A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BadRDM, and their shared main text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. However, v2 ends after its references and omits the Appendices A–C that it repeatedly cites; v3 includes Appendices A–F. This limits judgments about whether appendix-only material is newly introduced.

before.justification: V2 reports original class-conditional and text-to-image attack experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations and defense evaluations in Section 4, Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–5.

after.justification: V3 retains original attack experiments and reports revised defense results, with additional empirical results available in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The shared method retains contrastive poisoning, the benign alignment loss, text-encoder-only fine-tuning, minimum-entropy surrogate selection and generative surrogate augmentation. V3's pseudocode and additional retriever evaluations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: The visible coverage retains CC3M, ImageNet, OpenImages and MS-COCO, with class-conditional and text-to-image generation. Image-only conditioning and natural triggers were already mentioned in v2. V3 additionally documents a poisoned-retriever/clean-database deployment test in Table 11, but the missing v2 appendices prevent establishing whether this extends earlier coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains PoiMM, BadT2I (citing Struppek et al.) and BadCM. The defense comparison in Table 3 substantially expands beyond BFT and CleanCLIP by evaluating Unlearning, UFID and TextPerturb.

E3.justification: The shared training data, optimization settings, four-neighbor default and 20K-image FID evaluation remain consistent. Table 3 changes from three metrics for both generation tasks to five metrics for text-to-image defense evaluation, adding CLIP-FID and CLIP-Benign. V2 specifies two random targets per task; v3 does not specify the revised defense target count, so matched evaluation conditions cannot be assumed.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 expands robustness testing from two fine-tuning defenses to include unlearning, query detection and text perturbation, substantially broadening the countermeasure questions examined. The shared TSE, retrieval-number, trigger-number and loss-weight ablations remain unchanged. V3 also supplies auditing, architecture, poisoning-rate and deployment analyses, whose complete earlier status cannot be checked without v2's appendices.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix B.1 explicitly states that all experiments were run only once. V2's corresponding implementation appendix is missing, preventing a reliable determination of whether this is new run-count disclosure. The shared main results provide point estimates without uncertainty intervals; there is no evidence of increased replication.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the shared figures retain their results, but Table 3 substantially changes. Reported T2I BFT ASR changes from 0.942 to 0.8096 and CleanCLIP from 0.946 to 0.9032; new results include UFID at 0.4048, Unlearning at 0.9015 and TextPerturb at 0.9633. Class-conditional defense results disappear from the corresponding comparison. These are replaced and newly reported results, not established same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: The shared inference equation, contrastive and benign losses, combined optimization objective and entropy-selection formulation retain their mathematical substance. Embedding shorthand and clarification of the four selected surrogates do not introduce new theoretical reasoning. V3 adds no theorem or proof.

C1.justification: V3 explicitly includes effectiveness under common defenses among the abstract's central claims. The principal contributions remain the first RDM backdoor investigation, contactless poisoning through retrieval components, contrastive injection and two surrogate-enhancement strategies.

C2.justification: V2 emphasizes persistent attack success above 94% under its tested defenses; v3 gives a more differentiated interpretation, acknowledging UFID's mitigation potential and explaining the utility costs of other defenses. The new Limitations section also discloses occasional mode collapse, required retraining and increased instability at higher learning rates, substantially qualifying the method's practical reliability.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-repository link and supplies pseudocode, optimizer and hardware details, sampling settings, the evaluator prompt and target lists in its appendices. The previously visible epoch count, learning rate and loss-weight schedule are retained in Appendix B.1. Because v2's referenced implementation appendix is absent, the extent of genuinely new reproducibility information cannot be reliably separated from previously referenced details.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially revised: Section 2.1 removes the general diffusion-model and GAN background, while Section 2.2 expands security-related citations. V3 also incorporates defense literature for UFID, TextPerturb and unlearning, and cites BadRAG and PoisonedRAG when grounding its threat model. The claimed first investigation of RDM backdoors remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 extensively condenses and rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and experimental narrative. It changes the title, author/contact text and citation style, moves training details into Appendix B, and introduces dedicated Limitations and Ethical Statement sections. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V3 reformats the document's page geometry, typography and table presentation, and redesigns Table 3 from two task blocks into a T2I-only five-metric comparison. Figures 1–5 retain the same graphics. Its included appendices substantially expand the presented displays with Algorithm 1, Tables 4–11 and Figures 6–11, although their earlier counterparts cannot be checked.

improvement.justification: The broader defense evaluation improves the paper by exposing a meaningful countermeasure: UFID reduces reported ASR to 0.4048, producing a more qualified account than v2's uniformly high success under tested defenses. Explicit mode-collapse limitations also improve transparency. These gains are tempered by the removal of class-conditional defense results, unclear comparability of replacement scores and inconsistent poisoning-rate/database-size statements in Appendix C.5. Missing v2 appendices limit how much supplementary material can be credited as an improvement.
